Techniques Used: Generalized additive model with random intercept year effects (GAMYE)
Object detection (Faster R-CNN with ResNet101-FPN backbone)
Pearson correlation tests (on differenced time series)
Data & Platforms: Purple Martin Conservation Association (PMCA) project MartinRoost
Application Areas: Species Identification in Remote Sensing Data
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Data Integration and Fusion: Combining multiple, disparate data types (e.g., remote sensing, tracking, citizen science, climate models) to answer complex questions that a single dataset cannot. (e.g., Merging AI-detected roost locations from weather radar (NEXRAD) with ground-truth community science checklists (eBird) to validate the species responsible for the radar signals. Also, coupling radar-derived roosting phenology with large-scale gridded climate data (NCEP Reanalysis) to identify environmental drivers ).

Automation of Data Extraction: Using machine learning and computer vision to automatically identify, quantify, and track biological events from massive, raw datasets. (e.g., Applying an AI (Faster R-CNN) to detect and track the "doughnut-shaped" signatures of bird roosts from millions of archived weather radar scans, reducing human annotation time by an estimated 7x. Also, using an automated video analysis workflow (LunAero) to detect birds flying across the moon at night).

Spatiotemporal Linkage Analysis: Examining how environmental drivers or biological events in one location and time (distant) influence biological outcomes in another location and time (local). (e.g., Using a spatially explicit time-window analysis to find that warmer minimum temperatures in Alberta (a distant breeding ground) in mid-July advanced the postbreeding roosting phenology observed at the Great Lakes. Also, using migratory connectivity (MC) to link breeding and non-breeding populations to see if spatially separate groups experience unique threats).

Methodological Validation and Comparison: Rigorously comparing the outputs of a new or automated method against established data sources or expert knowledge to quantify its accuracy, biases, and utility. (e.g., Comparing three different methods for defining shorebird management groups (expert-opinion, flyways, and unsupervised clustering) to see which one produced the strongest migratory connectivity (MC) and best explained differential population trends. Also, comparing the phenology of AI-detected radar roosts against the phenology of high-count eBird checklists to confirm the AI was capturing swallow/martin roosts).
Summary Description: Dr. Jeffrey F. Kelly specializes in Aeroecology and Migration Ecology, focusing on the annual cycle, population dynamics, and social behavior of declining migratory birds, including shorebirds and aerial insectivores. His research integrates data from remote sensing (NEXRAD weather radar), biotelemetry (satellite tracking), and community science platforms (eBird). He applies advanced computational techniques, including AI-assisted computer vision (Faster R-CNN) for automated roost detection, spatiotemporal time-window analysis to identify climate drivers, migratory connectivity modeling, and automated moonwatching systems. This work quantifies phenological shifts, population trends, and nocturnal behaviors to guide wildlife management and conservation.
